candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on Luke
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. 1 Th 5:17.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Luke's editorial introduction to the unjust-judge parable — 'he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint' (Lk 18:1) — Cyril reads the dei-pantote-proseuchesthai (it-is-necessary-always-to-pray) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of ceaseless-prayer (later codified by Paul at 1 Th 5:17 — 'pray without ceasing'). The grammatical necessity (dei) puts ceaseless-prayer on the same canonical level as 'must-be-baptized' and 'must-suffer'. Tewahedo monastic-prayer-discipline cites Lk 18:1 + 1 Th 5:17 as the canonical doubled-witness for the seven-fold daily office (Mäshafä Sǝʾatat) — seven daily prayer-points are the canonical operationalization of 'always pray, never faint'.

On Christ's command to the rich young ruler 'Yet lackest thou one thing: sell all that thou hast, and distribute unto the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, follow me' (Lk 18:22), Cyril reads the sell-all + follow-me as the canonical Lukan anchor of the monastic-vocation specifically (not universal divestment for every Christian — Cyril is careful here): some are called to total-divestment as a particular vocation, and the rich-young-ruler is identified as such a call-and-refusal narrative. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Lk 18:22 + Acts 4:34-35 (early-Jerusalem communal-divestment) as the canonical doubled-witness for the monastic vocation; the cenobitic-Tewahedo monasteries preserve the apostolic-divestment pattern.

The blind beggar at Jericho — 'Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me' — gives, for Cyril, the canonical short-form messianic address. The blind man sees by faith what the seeing crowd does not see: the Davidic sonship of the passing Christ. Tewahedo invocation of the Jesus-prayer preserves the blind-beggar address as one of its earliest canonical forms.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Luke's editorial introduction to the unjust-judge parable — 'he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint' (Lk 18:1) — Cyril reads the dei-pantote-proseuchesthai (it-is-necessary-always-to-pray) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of ceaseless-prayer (later codified by Paul at 1 Th 5:17 — 'pray without ceasing'). The grammatical necessity (dei) puts ceaseless-prayer on the same canonical level as 'must-be-baptized' and 'must-suffer'. Tewahedo monastic-prayer-discipline cites Lk 18:1 + 1 Th 5:17 as the canonical doubled-witness for the seven-fold daily office (Mäshafä Sǝʾatat) — seven daily prayer-points are the canonical operationalization of 'always pray, never faint'.

On the Pharisee's self-praising prayer 'God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are' (Lk 18:11), Cyril reads the Pharisee's-prayer as the canonical Lukan anti-model: addressed-to-God-in-form but self-praising-in-content. The prepositional pros-heauton (with-himself / to-himself — preferred reading) makes the Pharisee's prayer self-directed even in posture. Tewahedo confessor's-prayer-formation cites Lk 18:11 + Lk 18:13 (the Publican's prayer — seed γ.4.3) as the canonical Lukan doubled-witness of the two-prayer-patterns: the wrong one (Pharisee, self-praise) and the right one (Publican, 'God be merciful to me a sinner' — the Jesus-Prayer of Tewahedo monastic-spirituality).

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

The publican standing afar off, smiting on his breast, saying 'God be merciful to me a sinner' — Cyril treats this prayer as the canonical Lukan form of the Jesus-prayer: short, exact, self-acknowledging, mercy-petitioning. The publican goes down to his house justified, not the Pharisee. Tewahedo monastic prayer tradition preserves the publican's prayer as the canonical seed of the continual prayer of the heart.

candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's command 'Suffer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God' (Lk 18:16), Cyril reads the doubled-imperative (suffer-them + forbid-them-not) as the canonical Lukan anchor of paedo-receptivity and (in the wider patristic tradition) infant-baptism: children are not deferred until adult-comprehension but received-now into the kingdom. The kingdom belongs not to children alone but to those characterized by child-like receptivity (Lk 18:17). Tewahedo baptismal theology — practising infant-baptism (often on the 40th day for boys, 80th day for girls per Lev 12 + Lk 2:22-24) — cites Lk 18:16 as the canonical Lukan-NT anchor for the practice.
